subtopic: Kinematics and Dynamics of Circular Motion
stem: Define centripetal force.
solution:
**Centripetal force** is the force acting on a body performing circular motion, directed along the radius toward the centre of the circular path.

It is the force that continuously changes the direction of the velocity and so keeps the body on the circle; without it the body would move off along the tangent. Its magnitude is

\(F = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = mr\omega^{2}\)

It is not a new kind of force but a role played by whatever real force acts toward the centre in a given case: gravitation for a satellite, tension for a stone whirled on a string, and friction for a car taking a level turn.

subtopic: Nature of Light and Huygens' Principle
stem: Explain the construction of a spherical wavefront by using Huygens' principle.
solution:
By **Huygens' principle**, every point on a wavefront acts as a fresh source of secondary waves, called secondary wavelets, which spread out in all forward directions with the speed of the wave in that medium. The new position of the wavefront after a time is the surface that touches all these secondary wavelets, that is, their common tangent or envelope.

**Construction of a spherical wavefront.**

Let a point source S in a homogeneous medium send out light. After a time \(t\) the disturbance has travelled the same distance \(vt\) in every direction, so the first wavefront is a sphere \(AB\) of radius \(vt\) centred on S.

To find the wavefront after a further time \(t'\), proceed as follows.

1. Take a number of points \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) on the wavefront \(AB\). Each of these is a secondary source.

2. With each of these points as centre, draw a **hemisphere of radius \(vt'\)** on the forward side. These are the secondary wavelets, and the radius is the distance the disturbance travels in the time \(t'\).

3. Draw the surface \(A_1B_1\) that **touches all these wavelets** on the forward side. This common tangent surface is the new wavefront.

Because the medium is homogeneous, all the wavelets have the same radius, so their envelope is again a sphere centred on S, now of radius \(v(t + t')\). The wavefront therefore stays spherical and simply expands.

The backward envelope is discarded: no backward wave is observed, because the intensity of a secondary wavelet falls to zero in the backward direction.

At a very great distance from the source, a small portion of such a sphere is almost flat, which is why a distant source gives effectively plane wavefronts.

Obtain the differential equation of linear simple harmonic motion.
solution:
Consider a particle performing linear simple harmonic motion along a straight line, and let \(x\) be its displacement from the mean position at any instant.

By the definition of S.H.M., the restoring force acting on the particle is **proportional to the displacement and directed opposite to it**, that is, always toward the mean position:

\(F \propto -x\)

\(F = -kx\)   ... (1)

where \(k\) is a positive constant called the force constant, and the minus sign shows that the force opposes the displacement.

By Newton's second law, if \(m\) is the mass of the particle and \(a\) its acceleration,

\(F = ma\)   ... (2)

Equating (1) and (2),

\(ma = -kx\)

\(a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x\)

Since the acceleration is the second derivative of the displacement with respect to time,

\(\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} = -\dfrac{k}{m}x\)

The ratio \(\dfrac{k}{m}\) is positive, so it may be written as \(\omega^{2}\), where \(\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}\) is the angular frequency of the motion. Substituting,

\(\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} = -\omega^{2}x\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} + \omega^{2}x = 0\)

This is the differential equation of linear S.H.M. Its solution, \(x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)\), shows the motion to be periodic with period \(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\).

Define the current gain \(\alpha_{DC}\) and \(\beta_{DC}\) for a transistor. Obtain the relation between them.
solution:
**Current gain \(\alpha_{DC}\).** In the common base configuration, the d.c. current gain is the ratio of the collector current to the emitter current, the collector voltage being held constant:

\(\alpha_{DC} = \dfrac{I_C}{I_E}\)

It is slightly less than unity, typically between 0.95 and 0.99, because a small part of the emitter current is lost to recombination in the base and appears as base current.

**Current gain \(\beta_{DC}\).** In the common emitter configuration, the d.c. current gain is the ratio of the collector current to the base current:

\(\beta_{DC} = \dfrac{I_C}{I_B}\)

It is large, typically between 20 and 500, and it is what makes the common emitter configuration useful as an amplifier.

**Relation between them.** For a transistor the emitter current divides between the base and the collector:

\(I_E = I_B + I_C\)

Dividing throughout by \(I_C\),

\(\dfrac{I_E}{I_C} = \dfrac{I_B}{I_C} + 1\)

\(\dfrac{1}{\alpha_{DC}} = \dfrac{1}{\beta_{DC}} + 1 = \dfrac{1 + \beta_{DC}}{\beta_{DC}}\)

Taking the reciprocal,

\(\therefore \alpha_{DC} = \dfrac{\beta_{DC}}{1 + \beta_{DC}}\)

and rearranging the same relation the other way,

\(\beta_{DC} = \dfrac{\alpha_{DC}}{1 - \alpha_{DC}}\)

This last form shows why \(\beta\) is so large: as \(\alpha\) approaches 1, the denominator approaches zero. An \(\alpha\) of 0.99 gives a \(\beta\) of 99.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Specific Heat Capacity and Mayer's Relation
stem: Prove the Mayer's relation : \(C_p - C_v = \dfrac{R}{J}\)
solution:
Consider **one mole** of an ideal gas, and let \(C_p\) and \(C_v\) be its molar specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume.

**Heating at constant volume.** The volume does not change, so the gas does no external work and the whole of the heat supplied raises the internal energy:

\(dQ_v = C_v\,dT\) and \(dW = 0\), so \(dU = C_v\,dT\)   ... (1)

**Heating at constant pressure.** For the same rise \(dT\) in temperature the heat supplied is

\(dQ_p = C_p\,dT\)

This time the gas expands and does external work \(dW = p\,dV\). By the first law,

\(dQ_p = dU + dW\)

\(C_p\,dT = dU + p\,dV\)

The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so the same rise \(dT\) produces the same \(dU\) as in (1) whatever the path:

\(C_p\,dT = C_v\,dT + p\,dV\)   ... (2)

**The work term.** For one mole the ideal gas equation is

\(pV = RT\)

Differentiating at constant pressure,

\(p\,dV = R\,dT\)   ... (3)

**Result.** Substituting (3) into (2),

\(C_p\,dT = C_v\,dT + R\,dT\)

Dividing throughout by \(dT\),

\(C_p - C_v = R\)

When the two specific heats are measured in heat units while \(R\) is in work units, the mechanical equivalent of heat \(J\) converts between them, giving the form asked for:

\(\therefore C_p - C_v = \dfrac{R}{J}\)

This is Mayer's relation. It shows that \(C_p\) always exceeds \(C_v\), because heating at constant pressure has to supply the extra energy the gas spends in pushing back the surroundings, and that the excess is the same for every ideal gas.
